content.thinking:
I'm drafting the symptom statement for the postmortem — account pages failing for many shoppers — then building the causal chain starting with the error rate spike, referencing the relevant incident and alert sources.

Next I'm pinning the immediate cause: account page requests hitting a ZeroDivisionError in the spend summary code starting at 10:00. Then I'm tracing the trigger back to the feature flag toggle, ruling out deploys and other production changes using the evidence (flag history shows only one change, deploy logs show nothing new, all replicas on one revision), and confirming the flag revert matches recovery — tying it all together with the relevant citations before moving to the next "why" in the chain.

Let me order the full chain: symptom pages failed, the ZeroDivisionError at line 47 got caught at the account page's request boundary and turned into a failed page, the flag-off change routed requests onto this path, and the function divides by this month's purchase count which is zero for shoppers with no purchases — it never handled that empty case. This reaches a root cause: turning off the legacy checkout fallback routes account page requests to the monthly spend summary path, which divides by an empty month's purchase count.

I'm phrasing the cause plainly: turning off a setting moved account pages to a newer monthly-spend summary method that apparently couldn't handle a shopper with no purchases yet this month, causing a divide-by-zero failure. For still_at_risk, I'm noting the underlying flaw remains in the code, so re-disabling that fallback or any path using the monthly summary would likely cause the same failure again for shoppers with no purchases this month, and the lifetime average also still seems to raise for accounts with no purchases.

Looking at contributing factors, I note the flag change hit all production traffic with no staged rollout or safety gate — logs show it went from a small slice to fully off within a minute, with no evidence of a canary or error-rate check before full rollout. Had a staged rollout with an error-rate halt existed, it would have caught the issue at a small slice instead of full exposure.

Another gap is that no test covered the monthly-summary path for a shopper with zero purchases, so the defect stayed latent while the flag was live — that's addressed by the proposed fix adding tests. Finally, nobody was actually paged since the alert wasn't tied to on-call, meaning if the automatic revert from Argus had failed, there was no human backstop watching the mitigation.

Actually there's an existing test pinning that failure-propagation behavior deliberately, so changing it would go against design intent — I'll skip that as a finding. Detection timing checks out fine (alert at 10:06, onset 10:00, with the rule's wait and window), so no issue there.

For action items, I'm drafting a prevent item around staged rollouts for flag changes that halt on rising error rates, plus a detect/process item linking the HighErrorRate alert to an on-call rotation so someone actually gets paged.

Noting what went well: Argus reverted the flag once the alert fired and confirmed recovery afterward, the investigator correctly pinned onset to the flag change and landed on the right single candidate, and Code-Fix already drafted a PR with a fix and tests.

What went wrong: nobody actually paged on-call despite the alert firing. As for luck, the revert only worked because the legacy fallback path hadn't been removed yet and was still healthy with the flag on — if it had already been deleted there'd have been no quick way back, so I should flag that cautiously as a lucky break rather than a guaranteed safety net.

On the assumptions side, I'm leaning on the idea that failing requests were shoppers with no purchases this month, but that's unmeasured and rests on an earlier inference. Customer loss estimates are also just comparisons against prior weeks, and the exact timing of when traffic fully shifted doesn't really matter here.

For ruling out other causes, deploy logs show nothing came back and the flag switch was the only production change on record, and the flag provider's history shows just one change in the hour before — which I'm assuming is this same change since no earlier changes exist to contradict it.

For the symptom step, I'm comparing error rates at their worst versus baseline, and noting that the first thing worth stating is what users actually experienced. The detail about all replicas running one revision as of a certain timestamp isn't necessary to include. Time to write this up.

action_items.item: Make changes to io-shop feature flags such as legacy-checkout-fallback roll out to traffic in stages, halting automatically when the account page error rate rises.
Route the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account pages failed. The share of requests to the service that failed rose from {errors_before} before the onset to {errors_while_broken} on average, peaking at {errors_at_worst}, and the service's own account page error-rate warnings peaked at {Gbac1.5}.

From the onset, account page requests raised ZeroDivisionError (division by zero) in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, at the line Code-Fix reads as line {F1.1}. Code-Fix's reading says the account page's request handler catches this error and returns a failed page.

ruled_out.what: A deployment. Deploys were read and none came back, and the only production change read was the flag switch.
Another flag change. The flag provider's history showed a single flag change by anyone but Argus in the hour before.

causal_chain.step: The requests reached that code because an admin switched the feature flag legacy-checkout-fallback off at {P1.1}. Before the switch, the logs show the flag on and account pages rendering normally. In the minute of the switch, most evaluations came back off, and from the next minute all of them did. Turning the flag back on brought the service back from the incident's level, and that revert was confirmed.

With the flag off, the account page renders the monthly spend summary. Code-Fix reads `average_spend_per_item_this_month` as dividing the shopper's month total by the length of the list of this month's purchases. That list is empty for a shopper who has bought nothing this month, which is normal, so the division raises. Code-Fix reads the function as never having handled an empty month: switching the flag only moved requests onto it.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Switching off an old fallback setting moved shoppers' account pages onto a newer way of working out monthly spending, and that code divided by zero and failed the page, likely for every shopper who had not bought anything yet this month.

contributing_factors.factor: No check or staged rollout was seen on the switch of legacy-checkout-fallback: within about a minute it went from most evaluations off to all of them off on live traffic.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A switch rolled out in stages, halting on a rise in account page errors, would have stopped while only a small slice of shoppers was affected, instead of failing pages across all traffic.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No test was seen exercising the monthly spend summary for a shopper with no purchases this month, so the fault on the flag-off path went unnoticed while the flag was on.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Such a test would have exposed the division by zero before the flag was switched off, and the switch would not have failed account pages.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

got_lucky: The legacy fallback path was still in place and healthy, as the logs from before the switch show, so turning the flag back on restored the service. Had it already been removed, there would have been no quick way back.
went_well: The Investigator dated the onset to the same minute as the flag switch and formed a single candidate cause, which the revert confirmed.

The Mitigation Agent switched legacy-checkout-fallback back on {T18.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, and confirmed {T21.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised that the service was no longer at the incident's level.
Code-Fix opened draft pull request #382, which proposes a fix with new tests, {T23.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
went_wrong: Nobody was paged: the alert was not linked to any on-call incident, so no person was brought in to oversee the automatic response or take over had it failed.

input.root_cause: Turning legacy-checkout-fallback off sent account page requests down the monthly spend summary path. There, `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py divides the shopper's month total by the number of purchases made this month (line {F1.1}). For a shopper who has bought nothing yet this month, that number is zero, so the function raises ZeroDivisionError and `serve_account_page` returns a failed page.
input.still_at_risk: The flaw in the monthly spend summary was still in the code, so switching legacy-checkout-fallback off again would likely make account pages fail again for shoppers with no purchases this month.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for many shoppers
